rulings.rationale: All actions for move 1 are mutually compatible and interact through the mechanism of constrained Starbucks mobile slot availability, competitive offers by Dunkin and Dutch Bros, and customer occasion-based switching (commuter, habitual app, café). No actual measurement exists; all outcomes are simulated. The pilot policy will introduce a real constraint on mobile order slots at 50 Starbucks cafés during peak, causing some potential mobile customers to face delayed pickup times or no available slots. Per the buyer dossier, commuters and habitual app users have explicit time/delay ceilings. If these are exceeded, some will defect to competitors or alternative channels. Both Dunkin and Dutch Bros are running targeted, limited-scope offers and/or labor increases in overlapping geographies, aiming to absorb some of this displaced demand. Walk-in café customers at Starbucks are unaffected or benefit. The magnitude of switching is not measured, so the outcome is branched by the realized rate of mobile customer defection and competitor absorption. No conflicting board deltas are proposed. All actors are affected; no kill criteria are triggered in this round.

chain.claim: Starbucks pilot policy reserves 20% of 15-minute peak capacity for café orders at 50 pilot cafés, capping mobile pickup slots and quoting later pickup times when mobile allocation is full.

Commuter and habitual app user occasions have explicit time and delay ceilings; if the Starbucks app cannot offer a pickup slot within those limits, the customer will defect to a competitor (Dutch Bros or Dunkin) if available, or choose an alternative channel.

Dutch Bros and Dunkin, in overlapping geographies, have both increased operational readiness (labor, offer, or marketing) to absorb some displaced mobile demand during the pilot window, but only within the scope of their local pilot actions.
Walk-in café customers at Starbucks are not negatively affected by the mobile slot cap and may see improved in-café experience.
